How to Choose the Right Metal Powder for Your Additive Manufacturing Application
Ask which metal powder is best for additive manufacturing and the most useful answer is probably another question:
Choosing a powder therefore isn't simply about finding the correct alloy. It's about matching the material to the manufacturing system around it.

Two powders can both be IN718, Ti-6Al-4V, or another established alloy while differing in particle size distribution, morphology, density, surface condition, and flow behavior. Those differences can affect how the material performs in the manufacturing process even when the underlying alloy chemistry meets the same specification.
Let the Manufacturing Process Narrow the Field
A prototype used for fit checks has very different consequences of failure from a flight-critical aerospace component, medical implant, or part operating inside an industrial gas turbine.
A powder that works for early development may not be the best choice if its availability, consistency, documentation, or production scalability can't support the eventual manufacturing requirement.

Let the Manufacturing Process Narrow the Field

Even narrow versus broad distributions involve tradeoffs. The appropriate choice depends on the balance of spreading, packing, feeding, layer thickness, and downstream processing required by the application.
A powder with excellent flow data isn't necessarily the best powder for a process. Neither is the powder with the narrowest PSD, the highest apparent density, or the most spherical-looking particles.
Lead times, batch flexibility, lot-to-lot consistency, feedstock availability, and the supplier's ability to support future requirements all become part of the decision as an application scales.
The Supplier Can Be Part of the Engineering Decision

A capable powder partner should be able to discuss the application, manufacturing process, desired PSD, material requirements, and likely tradeoffs. In development programs, that collaboration can help teams narrow the range of variables they need to test rather than treating powder as a fixed commodity input.
That is why powder characterization is such an important part of additive manufacturing.
That makes the test method itself part of the data. When comparing powders, engineers should understand not only the reported PSD but how it was measured.
Sampling Is Part of the Measurement

PSD tells one part of the story. Morphology adds another. Flow and density reveal aspects of physical behavior, while chemistry helps establish material composition and identify potential changes that can't be seen visually.
Sieving is an important part of many powder recovery workflows. It can remove oversized particles, fused material, and some forms of debris before recovered powder is returned to service.
